intro: A free meal served on the floor of a gurdwara in Palatine. A Jain monk sweeping the road before each step. A babalawo in Nigeria reciting verses he learned over many years. A crowd in white on a beach in Brazil, sending flowers out to sea. An Ojibwe grandmother in Chicago telling a story only in winter. This unit studies traditions that are smaller in numbers than the ones earlier in the course, but that shape the lives of millions of people and have left clear marks on Illinois and the wider world.

The first chapter studies Sikhism and Jainism, two traditions born in India. Each turns a central conviction into daily practice: for Sikhs, one God and the equality of all people, seen in the langar and the five Ks; for Jains, ahimsa, non-harm to every living being. The second chapter turns to traditions that keep what is sacred without a single book: Yoruba religion in West Africa, its descendants Santeria and Candomble in the Americas, and Native American traditions, including those of the Anishinaabe peoples of the Great Lakes.

By the end of the unit you will be able to explain the key terms and practices of each tradition, attribute beliefs to the people who hold them, compare how different communities answer the same question, and describe how laws in the United States have both suppressed and protected religious practice. You will also practice a skill this course keeps returning to: studying a tradition respectfully, including knowing when some knowledge is not yours to take.
bigQuestion: How do communities without a large following, or without a single sacred book, carry their deepest convictions into daily life and pass them to the next generation?

timeline.t: Mahavira, the twenty-fourth Tirthankara in Jain tradition, teaches in northeastern India
Guru Nanak, the first Sikh Guru, is born in the Punjab
The transatlantic slave trade carries millions of Africans, many Yoruba, to the Americas
Guru Arjan compiles the Sikh scripture and installs it at the Harmandir Sahib
Guru Gobind Singh founds the Khalsa at Anandpur on Vaisakhi
Sikhs believe Guru Gobind Singh names the scripture as the final Guru
The Treaty of Chicago: the Potawatomi, Ojibwe and Odawa cede their last lands near Chicago
Virchand Gandhi presents Jainism at the World's Parliament of Religions in Chicago
The first gurdwara in the United States opens in Stockton, California
Congress passes the American Indian Religious Freedom Act
The Supreme Court rules for the Church of the Lukumi Babalu Aye against Hialeah, Florida

words.d: the Sikh scripture, a collection of hymns that Sikhs honor as their living and final Guru
selfless service done without expecting reward; Sikhs regard it as a form of worship
the free community kitchen at a gurdwara and the vegetarian meal served to everyone, seated in rows on the floor
the community of initiated Sikhs founded by Guru Gobind Singh in 1699, whose members keep the five Ks
non-harm; the first Jain vow, extended to every living being, including the smallest
a ford-maker; one of twenty-four teachers who, Jains believe, show the way across the river of rebirth
the Jain doctrine of many-sidedness: any single statement captures only part of a complex reality
knowledge passed from person to person by speaking, singing and practice rather than by a written text
in Yoruba tradition and its diaspora, divine beings who carry out the supreme God's will and govern parts of life
a practice of seeking knowledge or guidance from sacred sources through signs, as in Yoruba Ifa
the rules a community keeps about how, when and by whom sacred things may be shared
the 1978 law declaring a U.S. policy to protect Native Americans' right to practice their traditional religions

test.q: Who founded the Sikh tradition, according to Sikh belief?
choices: Mahavira
Guru Nanak
Guru Gobind Singh
Kabir
test.why: Sikh tradition begins with Guru Nanak, born in 1469; Gobind Singh was the tenth Guru and Kabir a bhagat whose hymns are in the scripture.

test.q: Why do Sikhs treat the Guru Granth Sahib as a living Guru?
choices: Because it was found buried at Amritsar
Because it contains the Vedas
Because they believe Guru Gobind Singh gave the Guruship to the scripture in 1708
Because the Mughal emperor ordered it
test.why: Sikhs believe the tenth Guru ended the line of human Gurus and named the scripture as Guru.

test.q: Which practice best expresses the Sikh teaching that all people are equal?
choices: Eating the langar together in rows on the floor
Recitation of the odu
Fasting to the death
Sending offerings out to sea
test.why: In the langar, everyone sits in pangat and eats the same free meal, whatever their caste, wealth or religion.

test.q: Which of the five Ks is uncut hair?
choices: Kara
Kirpan
Kangha
Kesh
test.why: Kesh is uncut hair, usually covered by a turban; the kangha is the comb that keeps it neat.

test.q: Why does a Jain monk avoid eating root vegetables?
choices: Because pulling up a root kills the whole plant and small lives in the soil, violating ahimsa
Because root vegetables are reserved for the Tirthankaras
Because the Guru Granth Sahib forbids them
Because they are eaten only at Paryushana
test.why: Jains extend ahimsa to plants and tiny beings; uprooting a plant harms many lives.

test.q: How does the Jain idea of karma differ from the Buddhist idea?
choices: Jains see karma as fine matter clinging to an eternal soul; Buddhists see it as intention, with no permanent self
Jains reject karma; Buddhists accept it
Both describe karma as God's judgment
Buddhists see karma as matter; Jains see it as intention
test.why: Jain teaching treats karma as physical matter stuck to the jiva; Buddhist teaching treats it as intention and denies a permanent self.

test.q: Which statement about the two main branches of Jainism is correct?
choices: Svetambara monks wear no clothing
Digambara monks wear no clothing, and Svetambara monks and nuns wear white
The branches disagree about ahimsa
Only Digambaras accept the Tirthankaras
test.why: Digambara means sky-clad and Svetambara white-clad; both keep the five vows.

test.q: How did Jainism influence Mohandas Gandhi?
choices: Gandhi became a Jain monk
Gandhi founded the Jain Society of Chicago
Through his Gujarat upbringing and the Jain poet Shrimad Rajchandra, Jain ideas of ahimsa shaped his thought
Gandhi translated the Agamas
test.why: Gandhi grew up among Jains in Gujarat and credited Rajchandra as a major influence, though he remained a Hindu.

test.q: In Yoruba tradition, what is ase?
choices: A masked ancestor
A divining chain
A Candomble house
The power that makes things happen, coming from Olodumare
test.why: Ase is the power behind action and change; Olodumare is its source.

test.q: What makes Ifa an example of an oral tradition?
choices: Its verses are printed in a single holy book
Its thousands of verses are memorized and recited by trained babalawos
It is practiced only in writing
It was invented in Chicago
test.why: Babalawos train for years to memorize and recite the verses linked to the 256 odu.

test.q: Which diaspora tradition took shape in Bahia, Brazil?
choices: Santeria
Egungun
Candomble
Midewiwin
test.why: Candomble developed in Bahia in the nineteenth century; Santeria developed in Cuba.

test.q: Why did the Supreme Court strike down Hialeah's laws in 1993?
choices: Because they targeted one religion's practice while allowing similar nonreligious killing
Because Santeria was the city's official religion
Because animal sacrifice is required by the Constitution
Because the city had no council
test.why: In the Lukumi case, the Court found the ordinances were not neutral toward religion.

test.q: What does protocol ask of an outsider studying a closed Native ceremony?
choices: To record it secretly
To rely on what the nation has chosen to share and not imitate the ceremony
To buy objects used in it
To publish its songs
test.why: Respect for restricted knowledge means using what the community itself shares and leaving the rest alone.

test.q: Which statement about Chicago's Native history is accurate?
choices: No Native people have lived in Chicago since 1833
Chicago's name comes from a Lakota word for river
The Potawatomi founded the American Indian Center in 1833
After the 1950s relocation program, Chicago became home to one of the largest urban Native communities
test.why: The 1833 treaty forced most Anishinaabe west, but relocation in the 1950s built a large urban Native community in Chicago.

test.q: What weakness of the American Indian Religious Freedom Act did later laws address?
choices: It banned the Sun Dance
It applied only to Illinois
It stated a policy without strong enforcement
It required boarding schools
test.why: AIRFA set a policy but lacked enforcement; RFRA (1993) and the 1994 peyote amendments followed court losses.

write.prompt: How do these traditions pass their deepest convictions to the next generation? Choose two of the three: Sikhism, Jainism, or an Indigenous tradition from this unit. Cite a text, practice or law from the unit for each, such as the Guru Granth Sahib, the Acharanga Sutra or the 1978 AIRFA, and explain what adherents of each would say and why.
tips: Name the specific text, practice or law you cite, with its date where you know it.
Attribute every belief to its tradition: Sikhs believe, Jains teach, in Yoruba tradition.
Compare how the traditions answer the question rather than judging which is better.
Use the unit's terms, such as seva, ahimsa, oral tradition and protocol, and define them briefly.
For Indigenous traditions, name the specific nation or people and use only what they have chosen to share.
